title: The accession of the Emperor Justinian
shortBlurb: On the death of his uncle Justin I, Justinian became sole emperor of the Romans, beginning the reign that codified the law and warred to restore the empire…
body: On 1 August 527 the Emperor Justin I died at Constantinople, and his nephew Justinian, already crowned Augustus and co-emperor the previous April, succeeded him as sole ruler of the Roman Empire in the East. Born Petrus Sabbatius about 482 at Tauresium in Illyricum, he had long been the chief power of his uncle's reign; his consort Theodora had been crowned with him.

The thirty-eight years of his rule were the most brilliant of the later empire. His jurists under Tribonian gathered the law into the Corpus Juris Civilis — the Codex of 529, the Digest and the Institutes of 533, and the later Novels — which gave the canons of the first four general councils the force of law and fixed Roman jurisprudence for a thousand years. His generals Belisarius and Narses recovered Africa from the Vandals in 533 and Italy from the Goths in a twenty-year war.

He ruled the Church as he ruled the state, and not gently: the Fifth General Council, held at Constantinople in 553, sat under his hand and condemned the Three Chapters, while Pope Vigilius, kept in the city against his will, was brought to assent. When the Nika riot of 532 left the church of the Holy Wisdom in ashes, Justinian rebuilt it as the great church of Christendom. He died on 14 November 565.

title: Mary Tudor enters London in triumph
shortBlurb: Proclaimed queen against the nine days' reign of Lady Jane Grey, Mary Tudor rode into her capital to begin the Catholic restoration of England…
body: Edward VI died at Greenwich on 6 July 1553, and by his device the crown was settled upon his cousin Lady Jane Grey, proclaimed on 10 July. The country would not have her: the eastern counties rose for the Lady Mary, Edward's Catholic half-sister, and on 19 July the council in London proclaimed her queen. The Duke of Northumberland, the author of the device, was taken at Cambridge.

On 3 August 1553 Mary made her entry into London, riding with her sister Elizabeth from Aldgate to the Tower through streets hung for her welcome. At the Tower gate the prisoners of the late reign knelt to greet her — the aged Duke of Norfolk, Bishop Stephen Gardiner of Winchester, and Edward Courtenay, son of the Marquis of Exeter — and she raised them up and kissed them, and set them free. Northumberland went to the block on 22 August; the Lady Jane she meant to spare.

She was crowned at Westminster by Gardiner on 1 October. In the five years of her reign the Latin service was restored, the old heresy laws revived, and England reconciled to the Holy See; the fires kindled for the Protestants at Smithfield fixed her in the memory of their churches as Bloody Mary, a name her Catholic subjects did not use.

title: The election of Pope St. Pius X
shortBlurb: After the Austrian emperor's veto struck down the leading candidate, the cardinals chose the Patriarch of Venice, Giuseppe Sarto, who took the name Pius X…
body: Leo XIII died on 20 July 1903, and sixty-two cardinals entered the conclave at the end of that month. The favourite was his Secretary of State, Cardinal Mariano Rampolla, who took twenty-four votes on the first ballot; the Patriarch of Venice, Cardinal Giuseppe Sarto, had five.

On the second day of the conclave Cardinal Jan Puzyna of Kraków rose and, in the name of the Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria, pronounced the formal exclusion of Rampolla — the jus exclusivae by which the Catholic sovereigns still claimed a voice in papal elections. The cardinals protested the intrusion and went on with their ballots, but Rampolla's strength ebbed away, and on 4 August 1903, on the seventh ballot, Sarto was elected. He took the name Pius X, with the motto Instaurare omnia in Christo, 'to restore all things in Christ'.

He was crowned on 9 August. Among the first acts of his pontificate, by the constitution Commissum nobis of 20 January 1904, he forbade any such veto in conclaves to come under pain of excommunication; no secular power has openly intervened in a papal election since.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope St. Pius X (vatican.va)

title: St. Oswald falls at Maserfield
shortBlurb: The king who had brought Aidan and the monks of Iona to Northumbria was slain by the pagan Penda of Mercia, and numbered at once among the martyrs…
body: Oswald, son of King Æthelfrith of Bernicia, had spent his youth in exile among the Irish monks of Iona and there been baptized. Returning, he overthrew the British king Cadwallon at the Heavenfield near the Roman Wall, in 634 by the common reckoning, setting up with his own hands a wooden cross before the battle; and he sent to Iona for a bishop. In 635 Aidan came, and Oswald gave him the island of Lindisfarne for his see, translating the Irishman's preaching for his thegns until the English speech came to him.

For eight years he ruled Northumbria, the strongest of the English kings, whom Bede numbers among those who held the lordship of the southern nations. On 5 August, in 642 as the chronicle reckons, he met Penda, the pagan king of the Mercians, in battle at the place called Maserfield — Oswestry, Oswald's Tree, as the English came to name it — and was slain there, dying, Bede tells, with a prayer for the souls of his soldiers, which passed into a proverb.

Penda set his head and arms upon stakes. His brother Oswiu recovered them: the head was laid at Lindisfarne, the arms at Bamburgh, where his right hand, Bede records, remained uncorrupted. Miracles were told of the very soil where he fell, and the dead king was venerated as a martyr from that day.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 August

title: The death of St. Cajetan
shortBlurb: Gaetano of Thiene, co-founder of the Theatines and father of the clerks regular, died at Naples, worn out with labour and with grief for the city he loved…
body: Gaetano dei Conti di Thiene was born at Vicenza in October 1480, took the doctorate in both laws at Padua, and served Pope Julius II in the Roman curia before his ordination in 1516. In Rome he gave himself to the Oratory of Divine Love, a company of priests and laymen seeking the reform of the Church from within, and founded hospitals for the incurably sick at Vicenza and Venice.

On 3 May 1524, with Gian Pietro Carafa, Bishop of Chieti and afterwards Pope Paul IV, he founded at Rome the Congregation of Clerics Regular, called Theatines from Carafa's see — priests bound to common life and evangelical poverty, trusting in providence for their bread and forbidden to beg. Clement VII approved the order that June. It was the first of the congregations of clerks regular, the model of the Jesuits and the Barnabites that followed. In the sack of Rome in 1527 the little company was tortured and scattered, and made its way to Venice.

Sent to Naples in 1533, Cajetan laboured there fourteen years, preaching, hearing confessions, and founding a charitable bank against usury that grew into the Banco di Napoli. Worn with toil, and grieved by the factions of the city, he died there on 7 August 1547. He was canonized by Clement X on 12 April 1671.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 August

title: The death of the Emperor Henry IV
shortBlurb: The emperor who had stood in the snow at Canossa and warred for thirty years with the reformed papacy died an excommunicate fugitive at Liège…
body: Henry IV, king of the Germans from the age of six and emperor from 1084, spent his reign in the long quarrel over the investiture of bishops. Excommunicated by Gregory VII in 1076, he won absolution in the snow at Canossa the next January; then set up the antipope Clement III, took Rome in 1084, and was crowned by his creature in St. Peter's, while Gregory died in exile at Salerno.

His last sorrows came from his own house. His son Henry, crowned to secure the succession, turned against him, and at Ingelheim in December 1105 compelled the old emperor to resign the throne. Henry escaped his keepers, found loyalty at Liège and Cologne, and in the spring of 1106 worsted his son's forces near Visé; but his strength was gone, and at Liège, on 7 August 1106, he died, aged fifty-five, the ban of the Church still upon him.

Even his grave was contested. The faithful of Speyer bore his body home, but the excommunicate emperor was laid in an unconsecrated chapel outside the cathedral, and only in 1111, the ban lifted, did his son have him entombed in the cathedral beside his fathers. The conflict he had fought was settled eleven years after his death, at the Concordat of Worms of 1122.

title: The Robber Council of Ephesus
shortBlurb: Presided over by Dioscorus of Alexandria and backed by soldiers, the Second Council of Ephesus absolved Eutyches and broke Flavian of Constantinople…
body: The monk Eutyches, condemned by Flavian of Constantinople and his home synod in November 448 for teaching that after the union Christ had but one nature, found a patron in Dioscorus, Cyril's successor at Alexandria, and a court at his back. Theodosius II summoned a general council to Ephesus, and there, on 8 August 449, some one hundred and thirty bishops assembled, with Dioscorus presiding by imperial command.

The bishops who had sat in judgment on Eutyches were denied their votes; the letters of Pope Leo, borne by his legates — among them his dogmatic Tome to Flavian — were never suffered to be read. Eutyches was absolved and restored, while Flavian and Eusebius of Dorylaeum, his accuser, were deposed. When resistance was offered, soldiers and a monastic crowd were brought in; bishops were driven to sign a blank paper, and the deacon Hilary, the pope's legate, could only cry Contradicitur — 'it is opposed' — and flee for his life.

Flavian, beaten and sent into exile, died of his usage within days. Leo named the assembly a latrocinium, a den of robbers, and the name has clung to it. Two years later, at Chalcedon in 451, the work was undone, the Tome was read with acclamation, and Dioscorus was deposed.

title: The Battle of Adrianople (378)
shortBlurb: The Emperor Valens fell with two-thirds of his army before the Goths in Thrace, and with him fell the last Arian patron on the imperial throne…
body: Driven by the Huns, the Goths had begged admission into the empire, and in 376 the Emperor Valens let the Tervingi cross the Danube. The greed of the Roman officers starved them into revolt, and for two years they ravaged Thrace under Fritigern. Valens came up from Antioch and, unwilling to await his nephew Gratian's army from the West, gave battle on 9 August 378 near Adrianople.

The Gothic horse returned upon the Roman flank at the crisis of the day, and the army of the East was destroyed where it stood. Two-thirds of it perished, and the emperor with it; his body was never found. The historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who had marched in such armies, could find no Roman disaster to set beside it since Cannae.

Valens was the last Arian to hold the throne: baptized by the Arian Eudoxus, he had used his power against the Catholic faith in the East, driving its bishops into exile. The dead man's dominions fell to Gratian, who in January 379 called the Spaniard Theodosius to be Augustus; and Theodosius, within thirteen months, published at Thessalonica the edict that named the Catholic communion the faith of the empire.

title: The death of St. Flavian of Constantinople
shortBlurb: Deposed and beaten by the soldiers and monks of the Robber Council, the patriarch who had condemned Eutyches died of his usage in exile three days later…
body: Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople from 446, was the first to strike at the teaching of the archimandrite Eutyches, that after the incarnation there is in Christ but one nature. At his synod at Constantinople in November 448 Eutyches was condemned and cast out of his monastery; and it was to Flavian that Leo the Great addressed his dogmatic letter, the Tome, which the fathers at Chalcedon would receive as the faith of Peter.

At the council which Theodosius II gathered at Ephesus on 8 August 449, Dioscorus of Alexandria sat as president, Leo's letters were refused a reading, and Flavian was set at the bar as a criminal. Sentence of deposition was pronounced upon him amid the violence of soldiers and monks; the old man, clinging to the altar, was so handled that his strength was broken. He was sent into exile to Hypaepa in Lydia, and there, on 11 August by the ancient reckoning, he died of what he had suffered.

Rome kept him among the martyrs. When Theodosius died the next year, his sister Pulcheria had the body brought back to Constantinople with more honour, says the chronicler, than a triumph; and at Chalcedon in 451 his name was restored with praise as a confessor of the faith he had died for.

title: The death of Pope Innocent XI
shortBlurb: Benedetto Odescalchi, the frugal and inflexible pope who withstood Louis XIV and filled the war chest of the Holy League against the Turk, died at Rome…
body: Benedetto Odescalchi was born at Como in 1611, served the curia under Urban VIII, and was made cardinal in 1645. Elected pope on 21 September 1676 against the wish of Louis XIV, he took the name Innocent XI, cut the debts of the Apostolic Camera by rigid economy, and lived as plainly as he ruled.

His pontificate was one long resistance to the Most Christian King. He condemned the Four Articles of the Gallican clergy assembled in 1682; in the quarrel of the régale he refused institution to bishops who had taken part in that assembly, so that by 1688 more than thirty French sees stood vacant; and when the ambassador Lavardin entered Rome with seven hundred armed men to uphold the right of asylum, Innocent excommunicated him, and Louis answered by seizing Avignon. In the same years he condemned sixty-five lax propositions of the casuists and the quietism of Molinos.

The money his thrift gathered he poured into the war against the Ottoman: the subsidies he sent to the Emperor and to John Sobieski of Poland armed the Holy League that raised the siege of Vienna in 1683, recovered Buda in 1686, and took Belgrade in 1688. He died at Rome on 12 August 1689, and was beatified by Pius XII in 1956.

title: The encyclical Humani Generis
shortBlurb: Pius XII warned against new opinions in philosophy, Scripture, and theology, and ruled how far the question of human evolution might be discussed…
body: On 12 August 1950, addressing the bishops of the world, Pius XII published the encyclical Humani Generis, 'concerning some false opinions threatening to undermine the foundations of Catholic doctrine'. In that same year he would define the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin.

The encyclical warned against the fashion that would make dogma a mere symbol, against false irenicism that blurred revealed truth for the sake of reunion, and against the exegesis that emptied the first chapters of Genesis of history. On the question then agitating the schools, it did not forbid research and discussion of evolution touching the origin of the human body from pre-existing and living matter; but it required that souls be held immediately created by God, and it judged that the faithful could not embrace polygenism, which cannot be reconciled with the doctrine of original sin actually committed by one Adam.

Its cautions were felt as a check upon the nouvelle théologie stirring in France, and in the years that followed some teachers were withdrawn from their chairs. Several of the theologians so restrained were heard with honour at the Second Vatican Council, and one of them, Henri de Lubac, died a cardinal.

sources.text: Encyclical Humani Generis of Pope Pius XII, 12 August 1950 (vatican.va)

title: The election of Pope Paschal II
shortBlurb: A fortnight after Urban II died unknowing that Jerusalem had fallen, Cardinal Rainerius was chosen pope, to carry on the crusade and the Gregorian reform…
body: Urban II, the pope of Clermont, died at Rome on 29 July 1099, fourteen days after the crusaders had taken Jerusalem; the tidings had not yet reached the West. On 13 August the cardinals chose in his place Rainerius da Bieda, a monk from near Ravenna whom Gregory VII had made cardinal-priest of San Clemente and Urban had sent as legate to Spain. He took the name Paschal II.

His nineteen years were consumed by the same two causes as his master's. He forwarded the crusade, sending help to the new Latin kingdom and blessing the expeditions that followed the first. And he maintained the Gregorian law against lay investiture, coming to terms with Henry I of England and Philip of France in 1107, but finding no peace with the empire.

In 1111 Henry V came down into Italy, seized the pope and his cardinals, and after two months' captivity extorted from the prisoner a concession of investiture. A Lateran council the next year annulled the grant, and Paschal bore with patience the reproaches of stricter churchmen who blamed his weakness. He died at Rome on 21 January 1118; the long quarrel was composed four years after him, at Worms.

title: The Union of Krewo and the baptism of Lithuania
shortBlurb: At the castle of Krewo, Jogaila of Lithuania pledged his faith and his crown to Queen Jadwiga of Poland, and Europe's last pagan country was won…
body: On 14 August 1385, at the castle of Krewo, Jogaila, Grand Duke of Lithuania, set his seal to a solemn undertaking before the envoys of Poland: he would embrace the Catholic faith with his brothers and his people, marry the young Queen Jadwiga, free the Christian captives in his lands, and join his Lithuanian and Ruthenian dominions to the Crown of Poland for ever.

The word was kept. At Kraków on 15 February 1386 he was baptized with the name Władysław, on 18 February he married Jadwiga, and on 4 March he was crowned king. The next year he went up to Vilnius for the baptism of his people: the nobles one by one, the common folk in companies, while the sacred groves were felled and the temples of the old gods thrown down. A bishopric was founded in Vilnius in 1388.

So Lithuania, the last pagan land of Europe, entered the Church not by the sword but by a marriage; and the crusade of the Teutonic Knights, which had fed upon her paganism for a hundred and fifty years, lost its warrant. The union sealed at Krewo endured, through the nearer bond of Horodło in 1413 to the Commonwealth of Lublin in 1569.

title: The death of Wenceslaus IV and the Hussite storm
shortBlurb: The news of the Defenestration of Prague struck King Wenceslaus like a blow, and his death within the fortnight opened Bohemia to seventeen years of religious war…
body: Wenceslaus IV, son of the Emperor Charles IV, ruled Bohemia from 1378 and wore the title of King of the Romans until the electors deposed him in 1400. His reign fell in the worst of the Papal Schism, and in his kingdom the reformers preached to crowded churches: at the Bethlehem Chapel in Prague, Jan Hus denounced the wealth and vices of the clergy in the Czech tongue, and the king, for his own ends, had favoured him.

Hus was burned at Constance in 1415, and Bohemia seethed. On 30 July 1419 a Hussite procession in Prague, stoned from the New Town Hall, stormed it and threw the councillors from the windows to their deaths — the first Defenestration of Prague. The tidings came to Wenceslaus at his hunting seat, and the shock, it was said, struck him down; he died on 16 August 1419, aged fifty-eight, without an heir.

His brother Sigismund, whom the Czechs hated as the betrayer of Hus, claimed the crown, and the kingdom answered with war. Under Jan Žižka and his wagon-forts the Hussites broke every crusade sent against them, until the Compactata of Basel, granting the chalice to the laity, closed the struggle in 1436.

title: The Scots Confession and the Scottish Reformation Parliament
shortBlurb: In a week that ended a thousand years of the old Church in Scotland, the estates ratified a Protestant confession and then abolished the Mass and the pope's jurisdiction…
body: The regent Mary of Guise died on 11 June 1560, and the Lords of the Congregation, long in arms against her French garrison, made peace by the Treaty of Edinburgh in July. When the Scottish Parliament met at Edinburgh, the preachers were ready: John Knox with five colleagues — the 'six Johns' — had drawn up in four days a Confession of Faith on the Genevan model.

On 17 August 1560 the three estates, after hearing it read article by article, ratified the Confession as 'hailsome and sound doctrine grounded upon the infallible truth of God's word'. A week later, on 24 August, they finished the work: one act abolished the jurisdiction of the pope in Scotland, another repealed the old statutes in favour of the Mass, and a third forbade its celebration under pain of death for the third offence.

The young queen, Mary Stuart, safe in France as the bride of Francis II, refused her ratification, and the settlement stood without her. The Confession of 1560 remained the standard of the Kirk until the Westminster Confession displaced it in 1647; the old Church in Scotland never recovered.

title: The death of Pope Alexander VI
shortBlurb: Rodrigo Borgia, the ablest and most infamous of the Renaissance popes, died suddenly of fever, and his son's principality in the Romagna died with him…
body: Roderic de Borja was born at Xàtiva near Valencia on 1 January 1431, was made cardinal at twenty-five by his uncle Calixtus III, and for thirty-five years, as vice-chancellor of the Roman Church, served five popes with rare address. In August 1492 he was himself elected pope as Alexander VI, in a conclave tainted by promises and gifts.

His eleven years were spent in statecraft: he faced the French invasion of Charles VIII, excommunicated Savonarola, kept the jubilee of 1500, and by the bull Inter caetera of 1493 drew the line between Spanish and Portuguese discovery in the new world. For his children he was prodigal — Lucrezia in her marriages, Cesare in his carving of a duchy out of the Romagna — and the papal name sank to its lowest repute.

In the hot August of 1503 both father and son sickened after a dinner at a cardinal's villa near Rome. Cesare recovered; the pope died on 18 August, aged seventy-two. Men told of poison then and since, but the likelier cause was the Roman fever. Within months Pius III was dead in his turn and Julius II reigned, who broke Cesare and repaired what the Borgia had made his own.

title: The death of Blaise Pascal
shortBlurb: Geometer, physicist, and the fiercest pen of Port-Royal, Pascal died in Paris at thirty-nine, leaving in fragments his apology for the Christian religion…
body: Blaise Pascal was born at Clermont in Auvergne on 19 June 1623, a prodigy who wrote on conic sections at sixteen, built a calculating machine, and sent the barometer up the Puy de Dôme to prove the weight of the air. On 23 November 1654 he underwent the night of fire he recorded in his Mémorial, sewn thereafter into his coat, and gave himself to God and to Port-Royal.

For the Jansenists of that house he wrote the eighteen Provincial Letters of 1656 and 1657, published under a borrowed name, which made the casuistry of the Jesuits ridiculous to all France — and were answered by the Index and the bonfire. In his last years he gathered the notes of a defence of the Christian religion, published after his death as the Pensées, with its famous wager.

Frail all his life, he spent his strength in charity as readily as in thought: in 1662 he helped found the carrosses à cinq sols, the first public coaches of Paris, for the poor's benefit. Worn out by sickness of body, he died in Paris on 19 August 1662, two months past his thirty-ninth year, with the words, 'May God never abandon me.'

title: The death of Pope St. Pius X
shortBlurb: Broken-hearted at the coming of the Great War he could not stop, Pius X died in its first weeks, offering his life for the peace of the world…
body: In the summer of 1914 Giuseppe Sarto was in his eightieth year and the eleventh of his pontificate. The lamps were going out across Europe: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, Germany on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and Britain answered on 4 August, the eleventh anniversary of his election. The news fell upon the old pope like a sentence.

He sickened on the feast of the Assumption, 15 August, and in the early hours of 20 August 1914 he died of heart failure at the Vatican, whispering, it was reported, that he gladly offered his life for the end of the war. By his will his body was left untouched by the embalmers' knives and laid in a simple tomb in the crypt of St. Peter's.

The cardinals who gathered in his stead chose Giacomo della Chiesa, Benedict XV, whose whole pontificate was a plea for the peace his predecessor had not lived to see. Pius X was beatified in 1951 and canonized by Pius XII on 29 May 1954, the first pope so honoured since Pius V.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope St. Pius X (vatican.va)

title: The death of Alexander of Hales
shortBlurb: The English master who brought the Sentences into the schools and gave the Franciscans their first chair of theology at Paris died among his friars…
body: Alexander was born at Hales in the west of England about 1185 and went up to Paris, where he was master of arts by 1210 and regent master in theology a decade later, with a canonry at St. Paul's in London and the archdeaconry of Coventry to his name. King Henry III used him on an embassy of peace to France in 1235.

Then, at the height of his fame and past fifty years of age, he did a thing that astonished the schools: about the year 1236 he took the habit of the Friars Minor, and kept his chair. He was the first Franciscan to teach theology in the university, and among his hearers was the young Bonaventure. In his lectures he made the Sentences of Peter Lombard the text of the schools, as it remained for three hundred years.

His pupils called him the Irrefragable Doctor and the monarch of theologians. The great Summa that bears his name he left unfinished, to be completed by his brethren. He died at Paris on 21 August 1245, and the chair he had made illustrious passed, master after master, to the friars of his order.

title: The Battle of the Standard
shortBlurb: Under a mast bearing a crucifix and the banners of the northern saints, the levies of Archbishop Thurstan broke the invasion of David of Scotland…
body: In the anarchy of King Stephen's reign, David I of Scotland came down into England for the third time in 1138, professing the cause of his niece the Empress Matilda, and wasting the country south over the Tyne and the Tees toward York. Thurstan, the aged Archbishop of York, gathered the levies of the north to meet him.

The armies met on Cowton Moor, two miles north of Northallerton, on 22 August 1138. In the midst of the English host stood a cart, and on it a ship's mast, from which hung a silver crucifix and the banners of St. Peter of York, St. John of Beverley, and St. Wilfrid of Ripon — the standard that gave the battle its name. Thurstan, too old and sick to ride with them, sent Ralph, Bishop of the Orkneys, in his place, who absolved the host in the archbishop's name and promised the kingdom of heaven to those who should fall.

The wild charge of the Galwegians broke upon the dismounted knights and the arrows of the Yorkshire bowmen; the Scots were routed with heavy loss, and David barely brought his remnant back to Carlisle. By Michaelmas a truce was made at Roxburgh, and the north had peace.

sources.text: Richard of Hexham, De gestis regis Stephani (c. 1140), ed. R. Howlett, Rolls Series (1886)

title: The death of St. Philip Benizi
shortBlurb: The Servite general who had hidden in a cave rather than be made pope, and spent his office making peace between the factions of Italy, died at Todi…
body: Philip Benizi was born at Florence on 15 August 1233, studied medicine at Paris and Padua, and after a year's practice laid aside the physician's art for the new order of the Servants of Mary at Monte Senario. Ordained priest, he rose to be prior general in 1267, and governed the Servites for the rest of his life.

When Clement IV died in 1268 and Cardinal Ottobuoni named Philip in the conclave at Viterbo as a candidate for the papacy, he fled to a cave on Monte Senario and hid until Gregory X was chosen. He sat at the Second Council of Lyons in 1274, and in the faction-ridden cities of Italy he went about as a maker of peace; at Forlí, struck in the face by a young hothead named Peregrine Laziosi, he won him to penance and to the order, and to a saint's life.

At the chapter of 1285 his brethren, refusing his resignation, chose him general once more. Travelling, he came to Todi, and there, on the octave of the Assumption, 22 August 1285, he died. He was the first Servite to be canonized, raised to the altars by Clement X on 12 April 1671; his feast is kept on 23 August.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Servants of Mary (Order of Servites)”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 August

title: The death of Fray Luis de León
shortBlurb: The Augustinian poet and theologian, who had endured five years in the Inquisition's cells for a Spanish Song of Songs, died nine days after his election as provincial…
body: Luis Ponce de León was born at Belmonte in 1527, professed an Augustinian friar at Salamanca at seventeen, and rose to its most famous chairs of theology and Scripture, a Hebraist as well as the first lyric poet of Spain's golden age.

For translating the Song of Songs into Castilian and for questioning the received text of the Vulgate, he was denounced, and in March 1572 the Inquisition shut him in its prison at Valladolid. There, for nearly five years, he waited and wrote. Acquitted at last and restored to his rights, he went back to his chair; and tradition loves to tell, though the tale is not attested, that he resumed his lecture with the words, Dicebamus hesterna die — 'As we were saying yesterday...'

His prose works, the Names of Christ and the Perfect Wife, came out in 1583, and in 1588 he gave Spain the first edition of the writings of St. Teresa of Ávila. Chosen provincial of the Augustinians of Castile at the chapter of Madrigal on 14 August 1591, as he lay sick in bed, he died there nine days later, on 23 August, and was carried to Salamanca for burial, as his epitaph records, in his sixty-third year.

title: The death of Theodoric the Great
shortBlurb: The Amal king who had given Italy thirty years of peace between Goths and Romans died at Ravenna, and his work died with him…
body: Theodoric the Amal, a hostage at Constantinople in his youth and king of the Ostrogoths from 471, was sent by the Emperor Zeno against Odoacer, and after four years of war murdered his rival with his own hand at a banquet of reconciliation at Ravenna in 493. From that city he ruled Italy for thirty-three years.

An Arian among Catholic subjects, he kept the peace between them, holding that religion cannot be commanded. He governed through Romans — Cassiodorus his secretary, Boethius his master of offices — gave the land law in his Edict, restored its monuments, and left the Church to itself. But the last years darkened: on suspicion of dealings with Constantinople he sent Boethius and the senator Symmachus to their deaths, and Pope John I, come home from the East without the concessions he demanded, was thrown into prison, where he died in May 526.

Theodoric died of dysentery at Ravenna on 30 August that same year, and was laid in the great mausoleum he had built, under a dome of a single stone. His grandson Athalaric, a child, succeeded under the regency of Amalasuntha; and within nine years Justinian's armies landed, to undo the Gothic kingdom in a generation of war.

title: The death of St. Aidan of Lindisfarne
shortBlurb: The Irish monk whom Oswald brought from Iona, apostle of Northumbria and founder of Lindisfarne, died at Bamburgh, leaning against the wall of his church…
body: When Oswald of Northumbria asked the monks of Iona for a bishop, the first they sent came home in despair of the English temper; Aidan, trained under St. Senan at Scattery Island, answered that the fault lay with the messenger's harshness, not the people's. They sent him instead, and in 635 he was consecrated and set his see on the bare island of Lindisfarne, in sight of the royal fortress of Bamburgh.

For sixteen years he walked the kingdom on foot, the king himself his interpreter at the first, preaching and founding churches and monasteries; his school at Lindisfarne trained English boys for the ministry — Chad, Cedd, and Eata among them. The horse King Oswin gave him he gave to the next beggar he met. When Penda of Mercia heaped fire about Bamburgh, Aidan prayed from his island, Bede says, and the wind turned the flames back on the besiegers.

Oswin was murdered on 20 August 651, and Aidan outlived him by eleven days, dying at Bamburgh on 31 August, in the seventeenth year of his episcopate, leaning against a buttress of the church — a beam that, Bede notes, twice survived the burning of the church itself. He was buried at Lindisfarne, leaving to the English mission the memory, in Bede's phrase, of a pontiff of surpassing mildness.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 31 August
